stem:
A maternal–fetal medicine consultant reviews a singleton pregnancy at 31+5 weeks. Estimated fetal weight is below the first centile. Serial umbilical artery Dopplers have progressed from absent to persistent reversed end-diastolic flow, confirmed today. The CTG is currently reassuring. The mother is clinically well; corticosteroids are complete and neonatal intensive care is available.

Which timing plan is most appropriate to discuss?

options.label: A
options.text: Plan birth now following multidisciplinary preparation
options.explanation: At this gestation, persistent reversed umbilical flow is a reason to plan birth despite a currently reassuring CTG. Australian and SMFM guidance place this finding within an early-delivery window around 30–32 weeks.

options.label: B
options.text: Continue surveillance until 34 weeks if the CTG stays normal
options.explanation: A reassuring CTG is useful contemporaneous information but does not justify extending this reversed-flow pregnancy to 34 weeks.

options.label: C
options.text: Continue surveillance until 37 weeks if growth is maintained
options.explanation: Term-oriented timing applies to less severe growth-restriction patterns, not persistent reversed flow at 31+5 weeks.

options.label: D
options.text: Defer birth until the ductus venosus A wave becomes absent
options.explanation: Ductus venosus changes can inform very early FGR management, but waiting for that deterioration is not required at this gestation with reversed umbilical flow.

options.label: E
options.text: Wait for a non-reassuring CTG before recommending birth
options.explanation: Waiting for CTG deterioration adds risk when the Doppler findings already support birth planning; CTG is not the sole trigger.

context: At around 31 weeks, persistent reversed umbilical artery end-diastolic flow can justify planned birth even when the CTG is reassuring.
